facts.text: The 2026 improvement is a cash effect rather than deleveraging. facts.label: Contrary evidence and what would change the view
facts.text: The strongest evidence against a cautious view is the size of the equity cushion and the record of the capital structure. The equity price of about USD 4,801.08 million is 4.10x the existing debt principal, the reverse termination fee may point to committed financing, the 2025 amendment cut the term loan margin from 2.25% to 1.75% and extended its maturity to 2032-09-22, and the 2026 amendment enlarged an undrawn revolver to USD 850.0 million, which are not the actions of a stressed borrower. If the financing leaves the existing facilities in place with modest added debt, creditors could end up better protected by a better-capitalised owner. facts.label: Company description
facts.text: Option Care Health is a single-segment provider of home and alternate-site infusion services. It dispenses drugs and gives nursing support and care coordination to patients at home or in ambulatory infusion suites, and is paid mostly by managed care organizations, insurers, employers, Medicare and Medicaid. Net revenue was USD 5,649.519 million in FY2025 and the company reports 87 full service pharmacies and 188 suites. Cash flow is visible because chronic therapies repeat and the company positions home infusion as a lower-cost alternative to the hospital, but visibility is moderate: referral sources are not contractually obliged to refer, payer contracts can be re-bid, and acute therapies are episodic. These traits support debt service while payer terms hold, and they weaken refinancing confidence if margin keeps falling. facts.text: Until the merger agreement of 2026-10-05 the company was publicly traded with no controlling holder named in the filings supplied and no dividend ever paid. Business & governance assessed sponsor and governance risk as medium on the stand-alone record: no dividends, regular reporting and interim limits in the merger agreement, against buybacks above free cash flow in 2025. facts.label: Revenue drivers and pricing power
facts.text: Revenue is recurring in chronic therapies and episodic in acute care, concentrated in payer contract terms, partly regulated and exposed to published pricing benchmarks. Growth was 13.03% in 2025, with acute therapies growing at a mid-teens rate helped by shifts in the competitive landscape and chronic therapies at a low double-digit rate; in the first nine months of 2026 growth was 2.45%, with acute at a high single-digit rate and chronic flat as the chronic inflammatory portfolio declined on patient attrition and unfavourable mix. Pricing power is limited: reimbursement is set at a discount to average wholesale price or a premium to average sales price, payers can make the company bid against competitors, and direct government programs were about 12% of revenue in 2025 and about 13% in the nine months of 2026. Revenue is not structurally declining, but its growth has slowed and the 2025 acute surge may not repeat. facts.label: Cost structure and margin resilience
facts.text: Costs are mostly bought-in drugs, 70.84% of nine-month 2026 revenue, then salaries and benefits at 15.26% and other operating items at 6.96%, with SG&A at 12.1% of revenue. The filings do not split fixed from variable costs. Drug cost moves with volume and mix, so operating leverage comes from the labor and overhead base, which SG&A discipline has held to a falling share of revenue; but pass-through is limited because reimbursement follows benchmarks, and labor shortages have raised costs in some markets. Margins can be defended against modest volume pressure, but not against a payer rate cut, adverse mix or supplier price rise: gross margin has already fallen 3.55 percentage points from 2023 to 2025. facts.label: Capital intensity and cash conversion
facts.text: Capital spending was 0.73% of revenue in FY2025, so most EBITDA converts to cash before working capital: free cash flow was USD 217.14 million, 53.20% of EBITDA in FY2025, and 66.82% on the last twelve months, which includes the 2026 inventory release. Cash interest was USD 64.658 million in FY2025 and cash taxes USD 67.287 million. Operating lease liabilities of USD 104.70 million sit outside debt, and no finance leases, pensions, supplier finance or factoring were found in the sources. Payables are 1.64x inventories, so suppliers fund the inventory and shortening terms would call on cash. Quarterly operating cash flow swings widely, so seasonality matters for the revolver. The split between maintenance and growth spending is not stated, so room to cut capital spending is not established, though the amount at stake is small; EBITDA translates into durable free cash flow only if working capital does not reverse. facts.label: Competitive forces
facts.text: Rivalry is intense and fragmented: named competitors include units of UnitedHealth Group and CVS Health and other national and regional infusion companies, some owned by payers or distributors, which lets them price and source drugs more cheaply in some therapies; this pressures price and referral share. Entry barriers are moderate because pharmacy licensing, sterile compounding standards, accreditation and payer network access take time; the credit effect is that new entrants arrive slowly but integrated payers already sit in the market. Substitutes are hospital and physician-office infusion, which the company counters with ambulatory suites; they matter only if payers redirect volume. Buyer power is high: managed care consolidation and re-bidding limit pricing and can remove access to patients. Supplier power is also high: a few vendors supply most purchases, manufacturers can cancel contracts on minimal notice and some drugs have limited distribution. Together these forces explain a thin margin and mean the first strain on credit would appear in gross margin, not in liquidity. Basis: 10-K_2025-12-31_bios-20251231.htm.jsonl, pages 5–6; 10-K_2025-12-31_bios-20251231.htm.jsonl, page 8; 10-K_2025-12-31_bios-20251231.htm.jsonl, page 11; 10-K_2025-12-31_bios-20251231.htm.jsonl, pages 16–18

facts.label: External factors
facts.text: Regulatory and payer policy are material to credit and are run here; other categories are covered in less detail. Regulatory: Medicare payments face reductions of up to 2% a year through 2027, state Medicaid budgets are tight, and the 12% of revenue paid by direct government programs is exposed to fee schedules, audits and recoupment, while changes to the pricing benchmarks that set commercial reimbursement could reduce revenue per therapy across payers. Economic: the term loan is floating and the USD 300.0 million rate cap expires on 2026-11-30, so each 100 bp adds about USD 6.71 million of annual interest, small against EBITDA but real against free cash flow; labor shortages raise wage costs. Technological: the 2024 cyber incident at a third-party technology provider showed reliance on outside billing systems, and the company names AI adoption as a competitive requirement. Social factors are not a primary credit driver in the documents. facts.label: Strengths, weaknesses, opportunities and threats
facts.text: Strengths: scale and payer breadth, strong liquidity with a distant maturity wall, low capital intensity and positive free cash flow, moderate reported leverage before the merger. Weaknesses: thin and falling margin, supplier concentration, slowing growth with inventory-driven cash flow, and an asset-light balance sheet. Opportunities that could improve credit quality: acute and rare and orphan therapy growth, a possible payer preference for a lower-cost site of care, and equity-heavy merger financing that leaves leverage near today's level. Threats that could weaken it: payer re-bids and consolidation, benchmark or reimbursement cuts, biosimilar and chronic inflammatory mix shifts, buyout debt, and supply disruption. Basis: Business & governance (CP-1A); Financial foundation (CP-1); 10-K_2025-12-31_bios-20251231.htm.jsonl, pages 16–18; 10-Q_2026-09-30_bios-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 28

facts.label: Financial profile and credit quality
facts.text: The nine dimensions are assessed as follows. Scale and market position is strong: the company calls itself the largest independent infusion provider, revenue was USD 5,649.519 million in FY2025 and the national network spreads referral and purchasing. Competitive advantage is average: clinical capability and manufacturer access help, but payers can re-bid and referral sources are free to switch. Business diversification is average: payer and site breadth are good, but there is one segment, concentrated suppliers and no disclosed therapy mix. Cost and capex flexibility is average: capital spending is 0.73% of revenue so investment needs are small, but drug and labor costs are hard to reduce and the maintenance share of spending is not stated. Margin stability is weak: gross margin fell 3.55 percentage points over two years and a further headwind of about USD 55 million is expected, with EBITDA margin at 7.33%. Free cash flow stability is average: positive every year, 53.20% to 66.82% of EBITDA, but flattered by inventory in 2026. Ability to refinance is average: the term loan was repriced and extended in 2025 and the revolver enlarged in 2026, but no rating or market price is supplied and the buyout may change the structure. Liquidity is strong: USD 299.1 million of cash and USD 846.0 million undrawn, with no large maturity before 2029. Financial policy and governance is average on the stand-alone record, with buybacks above free cash flow in 2025 offset by no dividends and effective controls; after closing it cannot be assessed. Main supports are liquidity, cover and payer breadth; the main constraints are margin and the unsized buyout; the trend in margin is down and in leverage is stable; the missing datapoints are the buyout financing, covenants and therapy-level economics. Basis: calculation C2; calculation C3; calculation C4; calculation C8; calculation C10; Business & governance (CP-1A); Financial foundation (CP-1)

facts.label: Outlook, tailwinds and headwinds
facts.text: Over 12 to 24 months the closing of the merger, expected in the first half of 2027, dominates. Operationally, the last guidance of USD 5.675 billion to USD 5.775 billion of revenue and USD 480 million to USD 495 million of adjusted EBITDA implied a fourth-quarter step-up from the third quarter, and it was withdrawn on 2026-11-04, so no company forecast is current. Company-specific tailwinds are acute therapy growth, rare and orphan and immunoglobulin growth, the Intramed Plus acquisition and lower interest after the 2025 repricing; headwinds are the chronic inflammatory decline, biosimilar adoption, transaction costs and the end of the rate cap, which raises exposure to rates. Sector tailwinds include the company's positioning of home infusion as cheaper than hospital care, which payers may favour; headwinds are payer consolidation, vertical integration, reimbursement cuts and labor costs. Over three to five years the filings give no company outlook, so the medium-term view is not established beyond these structural forces. facts.label: Downside scenario
facts.text: The initiating condition is a payer re-bid or benchmark change that lowers revenue per therapy, compounded by the continued chronic inflammatory decline and biosimilar mix shift already flagged by management. The first operational break is gross margin: with labor and overhead assumed largely fixed in the short run (the filings do not split them), a one percentage point fall in EBITDA margin removes USD 57.52 million, 13.65% of last-twelve-months EBITDA. Financially, reported net leverage would rise from 2.04x to 2.36x, total leverage from 2.75x to 3.18x and cover would fall from 6.74x to 5.82x, with free cash flow lower and the 2026 inventory release not repeating. Liquidity remains ample: USD 299.1 million of cash and USD 846.0 million of revolver, with no large maturity until the 2029 notes, which equal 1.78 years of last-twelve-months free cash flow. Management levers are SG&A, inventory management and, until closing, the merger bar on buybacks and dividends; capital spending is already small. On the stand-alone structure resilience appears sufficient to avoid liquidity distress; the scenario changes sharply if buyout debt is added, because interest would take more of the lower EBITDA. The observable triggers are gross margin, payer re-bids, inventory-adjusted operating cash flow and the closing capital structure. Basis: calculation C2; calculation C4; calculation C7; calculation C9; calculation C10; Financial foundation (CP-1)

facts.label: Overall credit view
facts.text: Overall, Option Care Health presents an adequate business profile supported by payer breadth, scale and low capital intensity, but credit quality is constrained by thin and falling margin, supplier concentration and an unsized buyout. Cash-flow durability appears adequate: free cash flow was positive every year but the 2026 gain came from inventory. Refinancing capacity is likely to depend on whether the existing facilities stay in place at closing and on how much debt the new owners raise. The primary downside path is payer pricing and therapy mix eroding margin while buyout debt reduces the time to absorb it. Further analysis would require the merger financing papers, the credit agreement and indenture, covenant levels, ratings and peer data, and therapy-level economics. Top risk: margin erosion combined with any debt raised for the change of control. Basis: Financial foundation (CP-1); Business & governance (CP-1A); Source readiness (CP-0)

Top risk: margin erosion combined with any debt raised for the change of control.

## Findings
### Bottom line

The eight supplied filings and releases are enough for a financial, business and fundamental-credit review of Option Care Health, but they cannot support creditor-protection conclusions, because the debt documents and merger financing terms are absent.

Statements, the debt note and the liquidity disclosure through 30 September 2026 can each be traced to a page. On 2026-10-05 the company agreed to a take-private by affiliates of Clayton, Dubilier & Rice and McKesson at $32.05 per share in cash, expected to close in the first half of 2027. Neither the merger agreement nor its debt financing is supplied, so post-closing leverage, the treatment of the existing term loan and notes, and covenant headroom are not established. Adjusted EBITDA for FY2025 is also not printed, which rules out a trailing twelve-month company-defined figure, and no agency rating is supplied.

## Findings
### Bottom line

Reported leverage is moderate and eased in 2026, with net debt at 2.04x last-twelve-months EBITDA against 2.27x at year-end 2025, but the pending take-private makes that a historical reading, because the post-closing financing is not stated.
Basis: calculation C06; 10-Q_2026-09-30_bios-20260930.htm.jsonl, pages 21–23

Cash interest cover is 6.74x on the same basis, nothing beyond small term loan amortization falls due before 2029, and the revolver was enlarged in March 2026 to USD 850.0 million, leaving USD 846.0 million available after letters of credit. The 2026 improvement came from an inventory release and lower buybacks rather than debt repayment, since total debt barely moved, so it can reverse. Fiscal-year EBITDA is derived on the issuer's own definition, and no adjusted figure is stated for any full year, so adjusted leverage is not established.

Basis: calculation C03; calculation C05; calculation C06; calculation C10; 10-Q_2026-09-30_bios-20260930.htm.jsonl, pages 5–6; 10-Q_2026-09-30_bios-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 15; 10-Q_2026-03-31_bios-20260331.htm.jsonl, page 14; EX-99.1_2026-11-04_exhibit991-q32026.htm.jsonl, page 6

### Financial interpretation

Reported net debt to EBITDA rose from 1.52x at year-end 2023 to 2.27x at year-end 2025 and eased to 2.04x on a last-twelve-months basis at 2026-09-30; total debt to EBITDA moved from 2.25x to 2.84x and then 2.75x. The 2024 and 2025 increases came from capital allocation, not from falling earnings: buybacks of USD 252.726 million and USD 309.951 million, the USD 117.247 million Intramed Plus purchase in 2025 and incremental term loan borrowings of USD 49.959 million in 2024 and USD 229.472 million of new term debt in the 2025 refinancing (USD 180.239 million of old term debt retired) took cash from USD 343.849 million at year-end 2023 to USD 232.624 million at year-end 2025 while carrying debt rose from USD 1062.650 million to USD 1160.832 million. FY2023 is flattered: its reported EBITDA of USD 472.190 million includes the USD 106.0 million Amedisys termination fee, net of USD 21.1 million of merger expenses, inside Other, net of USD 89.865 million, and its operating cash flow includes the fee too, so the FY2023 ratios are not comparable with later years.

Basis: calculation C01; calculation C03; calculation C06; calculation C17; 10-K_2025-12-31_bios-20251231.htm.jsonl, page 53; 10-K_2025-12-31_bios-20251231.htm.jsonl, page 66; 10-K_2025-12-31_bios-20251231.htm.jsonl, pages 75–76

The 2026 improvement is a cash effect rather than deleveraging. Carrying debt fell only USD 2.998 million from year-end 2025 to 2026-09-30, while cash rose by USD 66.469 million in nine months: inventories released USD 63.104 million against a USD 24.899 million build in the prior-year nine months, buybacks fell to USD 170.545 million from USD 214.887 million and no acquisition was made against USD 117.247 million in 2025. A rebuild of inventory or a resumption of distributions would reverse it, and the merger agreement already bars buybacks without Parent's consent, which removes one use of cash while the transaction is pending.
Basis: calculation C02; 10-Q_2026-09-30_bios-20260930.htm.jsonl, pages 5–6; 10-Q_2026-09-30_bios-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 19; 10-Q_2026-09-30_bios-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 38

Coverage and cash generation are comfortable. Reported EBITDA covered cash interest 6.31x in FY2025 and 6.74x on the last-twelve-months basis; free cash flow after capital expenditure was USD 217.140 million in FY2025 (conversion of reported EBITDA 0.5320) and USD 259.407 million in the nine months of 2026 against USD 194.895 million a year earlier. The strongest contrary evidence to the view that leverage is a concern is therefore that cash interest is a small claim on earnings; what would make it win is a merger financing that adds debt, because none of these ratios describe the capital structure after closing.
Basis: calculation C06; calculation C14; 10-K_2025-12-31_bios-20251231.htm.jsonl, page 53; 10-Q_2026-09-30_bios-20260930.htm.jsonl, pages 5–6

Liquidity is ample and refinancing risk is distant. Cash of USD 299.093 million plus USD 846.000 million of revolver availability gives USD 1145.093 million at 2026-09-30, after the revolver was enlarged from USD 400.0 million to USD 850.0 million on 2026-03-30. Apart from term loan amortization of USD 6.780 million a year, the next principal due is the USD 500.000 million of Senior Notes on 2029-10-31, and the revolver springs to 2029-08-01 if the notes are still outstanding 91 days before they mature. Interest rate risk rises after the cap of USD 300 million notional expires on 2026-11-30: the whole USD 671.220 million floating-rate term loan is then unhedged, so 100 basis points adds USD 6.712 million a year, against USD 3.763 million with the cap in force at year-end 2025.
Basis: calculation C13; calculation C15; 10-Q_2026-09-30_bios-20260930.htm.jsonl, pages 15–16; 10-Q_2026-09-30_bios-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 30; 10-K_2025-12-31_bios-20251231.htm.jsonl, page 49

The merger is a subsequent event dated 2026-10-05 and is excluded from every period figure. The sources state a cash price of USD 32.05 per share and say Parent's debt financing is contemplated, but give no amount, lender or treatment of the existing term loan, revolver and notes, so pro forma net debt and leverage are not established and none is worked out here. Until the financing is known the observable test is the closing documents: whether the existing facilities are repaid or stay in place determines whether today's ratios carry over.

Trade payables are the main non-debt funding source: they rose from USD 426.513 million at year-end 2023 to USD 670.676 million at 2026-09-30 against inventories of USD 274.004 million and USD 408.045 million, and purchases are concentrated in three or four vendors. No supplier financing programme is disclosed in the sources read. If suppliers shortened terms the cash call would fall on working capital, so payables against inventory and vendor terms should be watched alongside cash conversion.

Data quality limits adjusted analysis more than reported analysis: statements reconcile in every identity, but the issuer states Adjusted EBITDA only for interim periods, so adjusted leverage cannot be built for a full year or for the last twelve months. FY2023 and FY2024 EBITDA growth is distorted by the FY2023 termination payment. A downside would run from slower acquisition of new patients or payer pressure to lower EBITDA, then to a cash cost if inventory has to be rebuilt, and finally to higher net leverage; the observable triggers are quarterly cash from operations, inventory days and the closing capital structure. No numerical stress is estimated here.
Basis: calculation C12; EX-99.1_2026-11-04_exhibit991-q32026.htm.jsonl, page 6; 10-K_2025-12-31_bios-20251231.htm.jsonl, page 71

- High: The issuer states Adjusted EBITDA only for the nine-month and quarterly periods of 2025 and 2026, and no full-year or fourth-quarter 2025 reconciliation is in the sources. A last-twelve-months or fiscal-year adjusted figure is therefore not calculable and adjusted leverage and cover are not established; reported EBITDA derived on the issuer's definition is used instead. The fourth-quarter 2025 release with the full-year reconciliation would close this.
Basis: EX-99.1_2026-11-04_exhibit991-q32026.htm.jsonl, page 6; 10-K_2025-12-31_bios-20251231.htm.jsonl, pages 52–53

- High: The financing of the merger is not stated, so the effect of the 2026-10-05 agreement on gross debt, cash and net debt is not established and no pro forma net debt or leverage is given. The merger agreement, its current report and the financing papers would close this.

- Medium: The revolver's security, legal rank and guarantors, the guarantors of the notes and the first lien term loan's floor are not stated in the sources read, so the revolver is left out of the debt stack and its rank is not established. The credit agreement, the indenture and the subsidiary list would close this.

- Medium: Source dashes are retained as missing, not zero: loss on extinguishment of debt in FY2023 and nine months 2026, proceeds from sale of assets and business acquisitions in the periods that print a dash, proceeds from issuance of debt, retirement of debt obligations and deferred financing costs where printed as a dash, and other noncurrent liabilities at year-end 2023. Reported totals remain usable; an explicit nil in the filings would close this.

- Low: FY2022 columns are not extracted and the quarterly columns of 2026 are not tabled; the three fiscal years and the nine-month comparison are the periods used, so older growth and quarterly seasonality are not established.
Basis: 10-K_2024-12-31_bios-20241231.htm.jsonl, pages 56–58

- Low: Fiscal-year EBITDA is derived rather than stated, and FY2023 reported EBITDA includes the USD 106.0 million Amedisys termination fee, net of USD 21.1 million of merger expenses, within Other, net, so FY2023 ratios and FY2024 EBITDA growth are not comparable. No house normalization is made.

- Low: Maintenance and growth capital expenditure are not split, cash restrictions on the balance are not stated, no pension or finance lease obligation was found, and the issuer's ambulatory suite counts use different definitions between the annual and quarterly reports. These limit capex intensity, net debt and operating KPI comparisons rather than the audited totals.

## Findings
### Bottom line

Option Care Health is a scaled, commercially funded infusion provider whose creditor risk now turns on its pending take-private, because control passes to a new owner group while its financing and the treatment of the existing term loan and notes are not stated.

Before the agreement of 2026-10-05 the shares were publicly traded with no controlling holder named in the filings supplied, no dividend had ever been paid, and cash went to buybacks of USD 307.5 million in 2025 and USD 167.5 million in the first nine months of 2026. Commercial payers supplied 86.78% of 2025 revenue and the largest payer about 14%, which spreads payer risk, but an operating margin of 5.76% leaves little cushion if reimbursement tightens. The merger agreement now bars dividends, buybacks, new debt and large acquisitions without the buyer's consent.

Basis: calculation C1; calculation C7; 10-K_2025-12-31_bios-20251231.htm.jsonl, page 37; 10-K_2025-12-31_bios-20251231.htm.jsonl, page 86; 10-K_2025-12-31_bios-20251231.htm.jsonl, page 10; 10-Q_2026-09-30_bios-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 34; 10-Q_2026-09-30_bios-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 38
### Key findings

- The take-private moves control to a private investor group on terms creditors cannot yet size. Affiliates of Clayton, Dubilier & Rice and McKesson would pay USD 32.05 per share in cash, about USD 4,801.08 million on the basic share count, which is 4.10x the existing debt principal of USD 1,171.22 million. Closing is expected in the first half of 2027 and either side may terminate if the deal is not complete by 2027-10-05. The agreement contemplates equity and debt financing, but no amount, lender or treatment of the existing term loan, notes and revolver is given, so the effect on creditors is open in both directions.
Basis: calculation C13; calculation C15; 10-Q_2026-09-30_bios-20260930.htm.jsonl, pages 21–23; 10-Q_2026-09-30_bios-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 35; 10-Q_2026-09-30_bios-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 37

- The buyers' willingness to support or extract from the company cannot be judged from the filings, and it is not inferred from who they are. No fund terms, equity commitment, fees or leverage plan are supplied. The termination fees are a partial signal: the buyer would owe about USD 291.93 million, 6.08% of the equity value, in specified cases including a failure to fund or close the financing, against about USD 145.96 million, 3.04%, owed by the company.
Basis: calculation C14; 10-Q_2026-09-30_bios-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 23; 10-Q_2026-09-30_bios-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 37

- Capital allocation favoured shareholders over debt reduction, and in 2025 it ran ahead of cash generation. Buybacks and the USD 117.2 million Intramed Plus purchase together were 1.97x free cash flow of USD 217.14 million in 2025, so cash fell and term debt rose on a net basis to fund the difference. In the first nine months of 2026 the USD 167.5 million buyback was covered by free cash flow, and none was made in the third quarter.

Basis: calculation C10; calculation C11; calculation C12; 10-K_2025-12-31_bios-20251231.htm.jsonl, page 53; 10-K_2025-12-31_bios-20251231.htm.jsonl, page 65; 10-K_2025-12-31_bios-20251231.htm.jsonl, page 86; 10-Q_2026-09-30_bios-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 19; 10-Q_2026-09-30_bios-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 34

- The merger agreement closes the main routes for cash to leave until closing or termination. It bars dividends, buybacks, certain new debt, certain acquisitions and capital spending above agreed amounts without the buyer's consent, and USD 525.0 million of buyback authority remained available at 2026-09-30. The protection ends if the agreement terminates, and the board raised that authority from USD 500 million to USD 1 billion in January 2026.

- Payer risk is spread, but the margin cushion is small and growth has slowed. Commercial payers supplied 86.78% of 2025 revenue and government payers 12.06%, rising to 13.03% in the first nine months of 2026 from 11.98%; the largest payer is about 14% and no other is above 10%. Revenue growth fell from 13.03% in 2025 to 2.45% in the first nine months of 2026, with acute therapies growing at a high single-digit rate and chronic therapies flat, and management expects the chronic inflammatory decline to cut 2026 gross profit by about USD 55 million.

Basis: calculation C1; calculation C4; calculation C5; calculation C6; 10-K_2025-12-31_bios-20251231.htm.jsonl, page 10; 10-Q_2026-09-30_bios-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 10; 10-Q_2026-09-30_bios-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 26; 10-Q_2026-09-30_bios-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 28

- Supplier concentration is a second operating dependency. About 57% of purchases in the first nine months of 2026 came from three vendors, against 68% from four vendors in 2025, and drug cost was 70.84% of revenue, so supplier terms largely decide margin. The company itself says a change in suppliers could delay service and cost revenue; the move from counting four vendors to three means the two shares are not strictly comparable.
Basis: calculation C9; 10-K_2025-12-31_bios-20251231.htm.jsonl, page 9; 10-Q_2026-09-30_bios-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 10; 10-Q_2026-09-30_bios-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 21

- Governance is conventional for a listed company and gives creditors no direct protection, while disclosure is adequate for monitoring. Eleven directors signed the 2025 annual report with a non-executive chair separate from the chief executive; directors can be removed only by a two-thirds vote, written consent is barred and undesignated preferred stock is authorised, which defends the board against bids rather than protecting lenders. Disclosure controls were effective at 2026-09-30 and no covenant waiver is described, but the credit agreement and indenture are not supplied, so covenants, guarantors and change-of-control terms are unverified.
### Contrary evidence and what would change the view

The strongest evidence against a cautious view is the size of the equity cushion and the record of the capital structure. The equity price of about USD 4,801.08 million is 4.10x the existing debt principal, the reverse termination fee may point to committed financing, the 2025 amendment cut the term loan margin from 2.25% to 1.75% and extended its maturity to 2032-09-22, and the 2026 amendment enlarged an undrawn revolver to USD 850.0 million, which are not the actions of a stressed borrower. If the financing leaves the existing facilities in place with modest added debt, creditors could end up better protected by a better-capitalised owner.

Basis: calculation C13; calculation C14; calculation C15; 10-Q_2026-09-30_bios-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 15; 10-Q_2026-09-30_bios-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 23; 10-K_2025-12-31_bios-20251231.htm.jsonl, page 75

Three outcomes would change the view. A financing that raises debt by a multiple of the existing USD 1,171.22 million, or repays the facilities without a change-of-control offer, would raise creditor risk; closing papers that leave the term loan and notes in place on unchanged terms would lower it; and a failed stockholder vote or regulatory outcome would return the company to a stand-alone issuer with USD 525.0 million of buyback authority still available and the 2025 pattern of shareholder returns ahead of free cash flow.
Basis: calculation C10; calculation C15; 10-Q_2026-09-30_bios-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 35; 10-Q_2026-09-30_bios-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 37; 10-Q_2026-09-30_bios-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 39
### Limitations

- The merger agreement, its current report, the financing papers and the proxy statement are not supplied, so the conclusion that the creditor effect of the take-private is open rests on a short note description; any financing amount or debt treatment would change it directly.

- The credit agreement, the indenture and the list of guarantors are not supplied, so the conclusions about change-of-control remedies, covenants and creditor control cannot be tested; a change-of-control put or default would turn the pending deal into a refinancing event.
Basis: 10-K_2025-12-31_bios-20251231.htm.jsonl, page 93

- Beneficial ownership, director independence and executive pay sit in a proxy statement that is not supplied, so the conclusion that no holder controls the company rests on the record holder count and the absence of any controlling holder in the filings supplied.

- Revenue by therapy, patient numbers and prices are not disclosed, so the margin cushion and the effect of the chronic inflammatory decline are judged from growth commentary and one management estimate of about USD 55 million, not from a mix table.
- The documents end on 2026-11-04, so the stockholder vote, regulatory approvals and any lender or rating action in the 14 days to 2026-11-18 are not covered.
Basis: calculation C20; 10-Q_2026-09-30_bios-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 40

### Transaction summary and new debt issues

On 2026-10-05 the company agreed to be acquired by an investor group of affiliates of Clayton, Dubilier & Rice and McKesson, through Onyx Bidco LLC, for USD 32.05 per share in cash. On the basic share count that is about USD 4,801.08 million of equity, 4.10x the existing debt principal of USD 1,171.22 million. The company would become a privately held, wholly owned subsidiary of the buyer and its shares would be delisted. Closing needs adoption by a majority of the outstanding shares, expiry of the Hart-Scott-Rodino waiting period and certain state healthcare approvals; it is expected in the first half of 2027, and either side may terminate if the deal is not complete by 2027-10-05.
Basis: calculation C13; calculation C15; 10-Q_2026-09-30_bios-20260930.htm.jsonl, pages 21–23; 10-Q_2026-09-30_bios-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 35

The company owes the buyer a termination fee of about USD 145.96 million in specified cases, including accepting a superior proposal, and the buyer owes the company about USD 291.93 million in specified cases, including a failure to fund or close the financing. Until closing the company may not pay dividends, repurchase shares, incur certain debt, make certain acquisitions or spend more than agreed amounts on capital projects without the buyer's consent.
Basis: calculation C14; 10-Q_2026-09-30_bios-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 23; 10-Q_2026-09-30_bios-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 37; 10-Q_2026-09-30_bios-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 38

The documents supplied say that equity and debt financing are contemplated but give no amount, lender, pricing or sources and uses, and they do not say whether the term loan, the 2029 notes and the revolver would be repaid, assumed or left in place. These are gaps, not conclusions, and no pro forma leverage is worked out.

No new debt was issued in the first nine months of 2026; the changes were to the credit agreement. On 2026-03-30 the revolver was enlarged by USD 450.0 million to USD 850.0 million, leaving USD 846.0 million available after USD 4.0 million of letters of credit. On 2025-09-22 the term loans were refinanced into a new First Lien Term Loan at Term SOFR plus 1.75% instead of plus 2.25%, due 2032-09-22, with USD 49.6 million of incremental term loan borrowing, and the revolver maturity was extended to 2030-09-22. The senior unsecured notes due 2029 date from 2021.

## Findings
### Bottom line

Option Care Health's stand-alone credit profile is adequate, with moderate reported leverage, strong liquidity and thin margins, but the pending take-private makes that profile historical because the post-closing capital structure is not established.
Basis: Financial foundation (CP-1); Business & governance (CP-1A)

Reported net debt was 2.04x last-twelve-months EBITDA at 2026-09-30, against 2.27x at year-end 2025, and EBITDA covered cash interest 6.74x; pro forma net debt after the 2026-10-05 merger agreement is not established. Cash and USD 846.0 million of undrawn revolver sit against only small amortization until USD 500.0 million of notes fall due in 2029. The weakness is margin, not liquidity: gross margin fell from 22.81% in 2023 to 19.26% in 2025, revenue growth slowed to 2.45% in the first nine months of 2026, and management expects a gross profit hit of about USD 55 million this year. The primary downside path is payer pricing and therapy mix eroding margin while any debt raised for the buyout shortens the time available to absorb it.

Basis: calculation C2; calculation C5; calculation C9; Financial foundation (CP-1); Business & governance (CP-1A); 10-Q_2026-09-30_bios-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 15; 10-Q_2026-09-30_bios-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 26; 10-Q_2026-09-30_bios-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 37
### Key findings

1. The stand-alone balance sheet is moderately levered and well covered, but every ratio predates the take-private. Reported net debt was 2.04x last-twelve-months EBITDA and total debt 2.75x at 2026-09-30, with EBITDA covering cash interest 6.74x; pro forma net debt and net leverage after the 2026-10-05 merger agreement are not established, so the ratios describe the issuer as it stood, not as it will be owned.
Basis: calculation C2; Financial foundation (CP-1); 10-Q_2026-09-30_bios-20260930.htm.jsonl, pages 21–23; 10-Q_2026-09-30_bios-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 37

2. Liquidity is the strongest support, and refinancing risk is distant unless the buyout financing changes the structure. Cash of USD 299.1 million and USD 846.0 million of undrawn revolver stand against scheduled term loan amortization of USD 6.78 million a year, and the next large maturity is the USD 500.0 million of senior unsecured notes due 2029-10-31, equal to 1.78 years of last-twelve-months free cash flow. The revolver matures 91 days before the notes if any are still outstanding, so the refinancing decision falls in mid-2029.
Basis: calculation C8; calculation C9; calculation C10; Financial foundation (CP-1); 10-Q_2026-09-30_bios-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 15; 10-Q_2026-09-30_bios-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 30

3. Margin is the weakest dimension: it has eroded for three years and a known headwind remains. Gross margin was 22.81% in 2023, 20.27% in 2024, 19.26% in 2025 and 19.0% in the first nine months of 2026. Management put the 2026 gross profit effect of therapy mix at USD 25 million to USD 35 million in the annual report and puts the chronic inflammatory decline at about USD 55 million in the third-quarter report; the two statements are worded differently, so the increase is indicative. A one percentage point fall in EBITDA margin would remove USD 57.52 million, 13.65% of last-twelve-months EBITDA, and lift reported net leverage from 2.04x to 2.36x; this is arithmetic, not a forecast.

### Company description

Option Care Health is a single-segment provider of home and alternate-site infusion services. It dispenses drugs and gives nursing support and care coordination to patients at home or in ambulatory infusion suites, and is paid mostly by managed care organizations, insurers, employers, Medicare and Medicaid. Net revenue was USD 5,649.519 million in FY2025 and the company reports 87 full service pharmacies and 188 suites. Cash flow is visible because chronic therapies repeat and the company positions home infusion as a lower-cost alternative to the hospital, but visibility is moderate: referral sources are not contractually obliged to refer, payer contracts can be re-bid, and acute therapies are episodic. These traits support debt service while payer terms hold, and they weaken refinancing confidence if margin keeps falling.

Basis: Business & governance (CP-1A); 10-K_2025-12-31_bios-20251231.htm.jsonl, page 5; 10-K_2025-12-31_bios-20251231.htm.jsonl, page 17; 10-K_2025-12-31_bios-20251231.htm.jsonl, page 52; 10-Q_2026-09-30_bios-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 22
### Ownership and group structure

Until the merger agreement of 2026-10-05 the company was publicly traded with no controlling holder named in the filings supplied and no dividend ever paid. Option Care Health, Inc. is the borrower and issuer, the term loan is secured by first-priority liens on substantially all assets of the company and its subsidiaries, and the notes are senior unsecured; guarantors are named in an indenture that is not supplied. Business & governance assessed sponsor and governance risk as medium on the stand-alone record: no dividends, regular reporting and interim limits in the merger agreement, against buybacks above free cash flow in 2025. The new owners, affiliates of Clayton, Dubilier & Rice and McKesson, have no behavior history in the sources, so their financial policy, dividend appetite and treatment of lenders are not established and are not inferred from identity.

Basis: Business & governance (CP-1A); 10-K_2025-12-31_bios-20251231.htm.jsonl, page 26; 10-K_2025-12-31_bios-20251231.htm.jsonl, page 37; 10-K_2025-12-31_bios-20251231.htm.jsonl, page 93; 10-Q_2026-09-30_bios-20260930.htm.jsonl, pages 21–23
### Revenue drivers and pricing power

Revenue is recurring in chronic therapies and episodic in acute care, concentrated in payer contract terms, partly regulated and exposed to published pricing benchmarks. Growth was 13.03% in 2025, with acute therapies growing at a mid-teens rate helped by shifts in the competitive landscape and chronic therapies at a low double-digit rate; in the first nine months of 2026 growth was 2.45%, with acute at a high single-digit rate and chronic flat as the chronic inflammatory portfolio declined on patient attrition and unfavourable mix. Pricing power is limited: reimbursement is set at a discount to average wholesale price or a premium to average sales price, payers can make the company bid against competitors, and direct government programs were about 12% of revenue in 2025 and about 13% in the nine months of 2026. Revenue is not structurally declining, but its growth has slowed and the 2025 acute surge may not repeat.

Basis: calculation C5; calculation C6; 10-K_2025-12-31_bios-20251231.htm.jsonl, page 10; 10-K_2025-12-31_bios-20251231.htm.jsonl, page 16; 10-K_2025-12-31_bios-20251231.htm.jsonl, page 42; 10-Q_2026-09-30_bios-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 26; 10-Q_2026-09-30_bios-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 28
### Cost structure and margin resilience

Costs are mostly bought-in drugs, 70.84% of nine-month 2026 revenue, then salaries and benefits at 15.26% and other operating items at 6.96%, with SG&A at 12.1% of revenue. The filings do not split fixed from variable costs. Drug cost moves with volume and mix, so operating leverage comes from the labor and overhead base, which SG&A discipline has held to a falling share of revenue; but pass-through is limited because reimbursement follows benchmarks, and labor shortages have raised costs in some markets. Margins can be defended against modest volume pressure, but not against a payer rate cut, adverse mix or supplier price rise: gross margin has already fallen 3.55 percentage points from 2023 to 2025.
Basis: calculation C5; calculation C17; 10-K_2025-12-31_bios-20251231.htm.jsonl, page 19; 10-K_2025-12-31_bios-20251231.htm.jsonl, page 42; 10-Q_2026-09-30_bios-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 21
### Capital intensity and cash conversion

Capital spending was 0.73% of revenue in FY2025, so most EBITDA converts to cash before working capital: free cash flow was USD 217.14 million, 53.20% of EBITDA in FY2025, and 66.82% on the last twelve months, which includes the 2026 inventory release. Cash interest was USD 64.658 million in FY2025 and cash taxes USD 67.287 million. Operating lease liabilities of USD 104.70 million sit outside debt, and no finance leases, pensions, supplier finance or factoring were found in the sources. Payables are 1.64x inventories, so suppliers fund the inventory and shortening terms would call on cash. Quarterly operating cash flow swings widely, so seasonality matters for the revolver. The split between maintenance and growth spending is not stated, so room to cut capital spending is not established, though the amount at stake is small; EBITDA translates into durable free cash flow only if working capital does not reverse.

Basis: calculation C8; calculation C12; calculation C16; calculation C18; 10-K_2025-12-31_bios-20251231.htm.jsonl, page 53; 10-Q_2026-09-30_bios-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 4; 10-Q_2026-09-30_bios-20260930.htm.jsonl, pages 5–6
### Competitive forces

Rivalry is intense and fragmented: named competitors include units of UnitedHealth Group and CVS Health and other national and regional infusion companies, some owned by payers or distributors, which lets them price and source drugs more cheaply in some therapies; this pressures price and referral share. Entry barriers are moderate because pharmacy licensing, sterile compounding standards, accreditation and payer network access take time; the credit effect is that new entrants arrive slowly but integrated payers already sit in the market. Substitutes are hospital and physician-office infusion, which the company counters with ambulatory suites; they matter only if payers redirect volume. Buyer power is high: managed care consolidation and re-bidding limit pricing and can remove access to patients. Supplier power is also high: a few vendors supply most purchases, manufacturers can cancel contracts on minimal notice and some drugs have limited distribution. Together these forces explain a thin margin and mean the first strain on credit would appear in gross margin, not in liquidity.
### External factors

Regulatory and payer policy are material to credit and are run here; other categories are covered in less detail. Regulatory: Medicare payments face reductions of up to 2% a year through 2027, state Medicaid budgets are tight, and the 12% of revenue paid by direct government programs is exposed to fee schedules, audits and recoupment, while changes to the pricing benchmarks that set commercial reimbursement could reduce revenue per therapy across payers. Economic: the term loan is floating and the USD 300.0 million rate cap expires on 2026-11-30, so each 100 bp adds about USD 6.71 million of annual interest, small against EBITDA but real against free cash flow; labor shortages raise wage costs. Technological: the 2024 cyber incident at a third-party technology provider showed reliance on outside billing systems, and the company names AI adoption as a competitive requirement. Social factors are not a primary credit driver in the documents.

### Strengths, weaknesses, opportunities and threats

Strengths: scale and payer breadth, strong liquidity with a distant maturity wall, low capital intensity and positive free cash flow, moderate reported leverage before the merger. Weaknesses: thin and falling margin, supplier concentration, slowing growth with inventory-driven cash flow, and an asset-light balance sheet. Opportunities that could improve credit quality: acute and rare and orphan therapy growth, a possible payer preference for a lower-cost site of care, and equity-heavy merger financing that leaves leverage near today's level. Threats that could weaken it: payer re-bids and consolidation, benchmark or reimbursement cuts, biosimilar and chronic inflammatory mix shifts, buyout debt, and supply disruption.
Basis: Business & governance (CP-1A); Financial foundation (CP-1); 10-K_2025-12-31_bios-20251231.htm.jsonl, pages 16–18; 10-Q_2026-09-30_bios-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 28
### Financial profile and credit quality

The nine dimensions are assessed as follows. Scale and market position is strong: the company calls itself the largest independent infusion provider, revenue was USD 5,649.519 million in FY2025 and the national network spreads referral and purchasing. Competitive advantage is average: clinical capability and manufacturer access help, but payers can re-bid and referral sources are free to switch. Business diversification is average: payer and site breadth are good, but there is one segment, concentrated suppliers and no disclosed therapy mix. Cost and capex flexibility is average: capital spending is 0.73% of revenue so investment needs are small, but drug and labor costs are hard to reduce and the maintenance share of spending is not stated. Margin stability is weak: gross margin fell 3.55 percentage points over two years and a further headwind of about USD 55 million is expected, with EBITDA margin at 7.33%. Free cash flow stability is average: positive every year, 53.20% to 66.82% of EBITDA, but flattered by inventory in 2026. Ability to refinance is average: the term loan was repriced and extended in 2025 and the revolver enlarged in 2026, but no rating or market price is supplied and the buyout may change the structure. Liquidity is strong: USD 299.1 million of cash and USD 846.0 million undrawn, with no large maturity before 2029. Financial policy and governance is average on the stand-alone record, with buybacks above free cash flow in 2025 offset by no dividends and effective controls; after closing it cannot be assessed. Main supports are liquidity, cover and payer breadth; the main constraints are margin and the unsized buyout; the trend in margin is down and in leverage is stable; the missing datapoints are the buyout financing, covenants and therapy-level economics.
Basis: calculation C2; calculation C3; calculation C4; calculation C8; calculation C10; Business & governance (CP-1A); Financial foundation (CP-1)
### Outlook, tailwinds and headwinds

Over 12 to 24 months the closing of the merger, expected in the first half of 2027, dominates. Operationally, the last guidance of USD 5.675 billion to USD 5.775 billion of revenue and USD 480 million to USD 495 million of adjusted EBITDA implied a fourth-quarter step-up from the third quarter, and it was withdrawn on 2026-11-04, so no company forecast is current. Company-specific tailwinds are acute therapy growth, rare and orphan and immunoglobulin growth, the Intramed Plus acquisition and lower interest after the 2025 repricing; headwinds are the chronic inflammatory decline, biosimilar adoption, transaction costs and the end of the rate cap, which raises exposure to rates. Sector tailwinds include the company's positioning of home infusion as cheaper than hospital care, which payers may favour; headwinds are payer consolidation, vertical integration, reimbursement cuts and labor costs. Over three to five years the filings give no company outlook, so the medium-term view is not established beyond these structural forces.

Basis: calculation C11; calculation C15; 10-K_2025-12-31_bios-20251231.htm.jsonl, page 5; 10-K_2025-12-31_bios-20251231.htm.jsonl, pages 16–17; 10-Q_2026-09-30_bios-20260930.htm.jsonl, pages 22–28; EX-99.1_2026-07-29_exhibit991-q22026.htm.jsonl, page 1; EX-99.1_2026-11-04_exhibit991-q32026.htm.jsonl, page 1
### Downside scenario

The initiating condition is a payer re-bid or benchmark change that lowers revenue per therapy, compounded by the continued chronic inflammatory decline and biosimilar mix shift already flagged by management. The first operational break is gross margin: with labor and overhead assumed largely fixed in the short run (the filings do not split them), a one percentage point fall in EBITDA margin removes USD 57.52 million, 13.65% of last-twelve-months EBITDA. Financially, reported net leverage would rise from 2.04x to 2.36x, total leverage from 2.75x to 3.18x and cover would fall from 6.74x to 5.82x, with free cash flow lower and the 2026 inventory release not repeating. Liquidity remains ample: USD 299.1 million of cash and USD 846.0 million of revolver, with no large maturity until the 2029 notes, which equal 1.78 years of last-twelve-months free cash flow. Management levers are SG&A, inventory management and, until closing, the merger bar on buybacks and dividends; capital spending is already small. On the stand-alone structure resilience appears sufficient to avoid liquidity distress; the scenario changes sharply if buyout debt is added, because interest would take more of the lower EBITDA. The observable triggers are gross margin, payer re-bids, inventory-adjusted operating cash flow and the closing capital structure.
Basis: calculation C2; calculation C4; calculation C7; calculation C9; calculation C10; Financial foundation (CP-1)
### Overall credit view

Overall, Option Care Health presents an adequate business profile supported by payer breadth, scale and low capital intensity, but credit quality is constrained by thin and falling margin, supplier concentration and an unsized buyout. Cash-flow durability appears adequate: free cash flow was positive every year but the 2026 gain came from inventory. Refinancing capacity is likely to depend on whether the existing facilities stay in place at closing and on how much debt the new owners raise. The primary downside path is payer pricing and therapy mix eroding margin while buyout debt reduces the time to absorb it. Further analysis would require the merger financing papers, the credit agreement and indenture, covenant levels, ratings and peer data, and therapy-level economics. Top risk: margin erosion combined with any debt raised for the change of control.
Basis: Financial foundation (CP-1); Business & governance (CP-1A); Source readiness (CP-0)
